translationRepairs: Yang Shihou came from Jinchou in Yingzhou.

斤溝 is Jingou, not Jinchou; the place-name romanization is wrong.
Yang Shihou, a man of Jinchou in Yingzhou.
Yang Shihou, a man of Jingou in Yingzhou.
斤溝 is Jingou, not Jinchou; the place-name romanization is wrong.
After Baixiang the Jin had harried the frontier; Shihou marched the main host to Zhenzhou, burned villages, raided Gaocheng and Shulu, and withdrew from deep in Zhao territory.

Earlier, after our setback at Baixiang the men of Zhen had repeatedly raided the border; Shihou led the main army straight to Zhenzhou below the walls, burned and swept hamlets, shifted the army to plunder Gaocheng and Shulu, and returned from Shenzhou.
深州 is the prefecture Shenzhou, not “deep”; 鎮人 are men of Zhen.

Earlier, after our setback at Baixiang the Jin had repeatedly raided the border; Shihou led the main army straight to Zhenzhou below the walls, burned and swept hamlets, shifted the army to plunder Gaocheng and Shulu, and returned from deep in Zhao.

Earlier, after our setback at Baixiang the men of Zhen had repeatedly raided the border; Shihou led the main army straight to Zhenzhou below the walls, burned and swept hamlets, shifted the army to plunder Gaocheng and Shulu, and returned from Shenzhou.
深州 is Shenzhou; both English fields mistranslate 深 as “deep”.
Yan failed to get in; Cunjie alone rushed the west gate with hidden men and scaling ladders, took the bridge, and the whole force poured in.
Wang Yan could not enter; Cunjie alone led the hidden troops bearing ladders in a mass assault on the west barbican, seized the moat bridge, and all armies advanced together.
王言 is Wang Yan; idiomatic “Yan” wrongly looks like the place Yan (鄆).
Born Li, he received the style Zanzhen from the Founder.
His original name was Li; the Founder changed it and gave him his courtesy name.
本名禮，太祖改而字之: the Founder changed his name and styled him; “Born Li” is unnatural.
In year 5 he became prefect of Bo, soon Xuanyi commander, then governor of Su.
In year 5 he became prefect of Bo, soon Xuanwu commander, then governor of Su.
Chinese 宣武軍 is the Xuanwu Army; Xuanyi is a wrong romanization of 宣武.
Year 5, he was made prefect of Bo; soon he was advanced to overall commander of the Xuanyi army and changed to prefect of Su.
Year 5, he was made prefect of Bo; soon he was advanced to overall commander of the Xuanwu army and changed to prefect of Su.
Chinese 宣武軍 is the Xuanwu Army; Xuanyi misreads 宣武.

The Jin were fresh from victory and fierce; Cunjie pushed on, marched by night with gags, and reached Ze as the wall guards were already firing beacons and shouting to the relief force; prefect Bao Ya stood in the city in confusion.

The Jin were fresh from victory and fierce; Cunjie pushed on, marched by night with gags, and reached Ze as the wall guards were already firing beacons and shouting to the relief force; the prefect held the yamen city and did not know what to do.
Chinese 刺史保衙城 means the prefect defended/held the yamen citadel; 保衙 is not a personal name Bao Ya.

At that time the Jin had just won and their edge was very sharp; Cunjie led his followers forward, marched at night with gags in the men's mouths, and reached Ze; he happened on the wall guards already lighting fires and shouting to answer the outside army; the prefect Bao Ya held the city and did not know what to do.

At that time the Jin had just won and their edge was very sharp; Cunjie led his followers forward, marched at night with gags in the men's mouths, and reached Ze; he happened on the wall guards already lighting fires and shouting to answer the outside army; the prefect held the yamen city and did not know what to do.
Chinese 保衙城 is 'held the yamen city,' not a person named Bao Ya.
In the fourth month of year 3 he was relieved as regent of Fuzhou.
In the fourth month of year 3 he was appointed regent of Fuzhou.
Chinese 除 means to appoint/install in office, not to relieve or remove from office.
Year 3, fourth month, removed as Fuzhou regent.
Year 3, fourth month, appointed Fuzhou regent.
Chinese 除鄜州留後 means he was appointed Fuzhou regent; 除 is not 'removed.'
In the eleventh month he was given the Golden Pocket, Honored Equal to the Three Dukes, a thousand-household fief, and the Yanzhou command.
In the eleventh month he was given permission to open an office with honors equal to the Three Dukes, a thousand-household fief, and the Yanzhou command.
Chinese 開府儀同三司 is Kaifu Yitong Sansi, not a 'Golden Pocket.'
Eleventh month, added Bearer of the Golden Pocket, Park-Walled Honored Equal to the Three Dukes, food domain one thousand households, appointed Yanzhou military commissioner.
Eleventh month, added Permitted to Open an Office with Honors Equal to the Three Dukes, food domain one thousand households, appointed Yanzhou military commissioner.
Chinese 開府儀同三司 does not mean Bearer of the Golden Pocket or Park-Walled.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor.
冊贈 is posthumous bestowal of an honorific title, not feudal enfeoffment.
He was posthumously enfeoffed Grand Preceptor.
He was posthumously granted Grand Preceptor.
冊贈 denotes posthumous granting of a title, not enfeoffment.
His father Huan was Chamberlain for Dependencies and, through Tan's eminence, was repeatedly promoted to Left Vice Director.
His father Huan was Chamberlain for Dependencies and, through Tan's eminence, was repeatedly granted posthumous promotion to Left Vice Director.
累贈 is repeated posthumous bestowal, not promotion of a living official.
His father Huan was Chamberlain for Dependencies; because Tan was honored, he was repeatedly advanced to Left Vice Director.
His father Huan was Chamberlain for Dependencies; because Tan was honored, he was repeatedly granted posthumous advancement to Left Vice Director.
累贈 marks posthumous advancement, which the literal English omits.
In year 4 Yang Yanhong of Bian defeated Shang Rang and Li Kan outside Weishi Gate; Tan fought in the van, broke the enemy line, won the Founder's notice, and rose in rank.
In year 4 Yang Yanhong of Bian defeated Shang Rang and Li Dang outside Weishi Gate; Tan fought in the van, broke the enemy line, won the Founder's notice, and rose in rank.
李讜 is Li Dang; Kan is a wrong reading of 讜.

Year 4, Bian general Yang Yanhong defeated Chao generals Shang Rang and Li Kan outside the Weishi Gate; Tan was in the battle, shattered the van and broke the array, and thus came to the Founder's notice and gradually received promotion.

Year 4, Bian general Yang Yanhong defeated Chao generals Shang Rang and Li Dang outside the Weishi Gate; Tan was in the battle, shattered the van and broke the array, and thus came to the Founder's notice and gradually received promotion.
李讜 should be rendered Li Dang, not Li Kan.

In the seventh month he received the Golden Pocket, Honored Equal to the Three Dukes, honorary Grand Marshal, and princely rank of Langya; Zhao Yinheng brought the edict, with a thousand bolts of silk and a thousand taels of silver for holding Xing.

In the seventh month he was further granted Kaifu Yitong Sansi (Honored Equal to the Three Dukes), honorary Grand Marshal, and advancement to Prince of Langya; Zhao Yinheng brought the edict, with a thousand bolts of silk and a thousand taels of silver for holding Xing.
開府儀同三司 is Kaifu Yitong Sansi, not a Golden Pocket.

Seventh month, again added Bearer of the Golden Pocket, Park-Walled Honored Equal to the Three Dukes, honorary Grand Marshal, advanced to Prince of Langya commandery, ordered Palace Commissioner Zhao Yinheng to convey the edict in comfort, and bestowed one thousand bolts of silk and one thousand taels of silver—reward for defending Xingzhou.

Seventh month, again added Kaifu Yitong Sansi (Unbridled Office with Honors Equal to the Three Dukes), honorary Grand Marshal, advanced to Prince of Langya commandery, ordered Palace Commissioner Zhao Yinheng to convey the edict in comfort, and bestowed one thousand bolts of silk and one thousand taels of silver—reward for defending Xingzhou.
開府儀同三司 is mistranslated as Bearer of the Golden Pocket / Park-Walled.
In the sixth month the Prince of Jin took Weizhou and seized its dependencies; Hebei was in turmoil; Tan was ordered to advance with Liu Zhen of Kaifeng in support of Hebei.
In the sixth month the Prince of Jin took Weizhou and seized its dependencies; Hebei was in turmoil; Tan was ordered to advance with Liu Xun of Kaifeng in support of Hebei.
Chinese 劉鄩 is Liu Xun (鄩 = Xún); the idiomatic English wrongly renders the given name as Zhen.

Sixth month, the Prince of Jin entered Weizhou and sent troops in divisions to take subordinate commanderies; Hebei was greatly disturbed; Tan received an edict with Kaifeng Intendant Liu Zhen to advance in pincer and aid Hebei.

Sixth month, the Prince of Jin entered Weizhou and sent troops in divisions to take subordinate commanderies; Hebei was greatly disturbed; Tan received an edict with Kaifeng Intendant Liu Xun to advance in pincer and aid Hebei.
Chinese 劉鄩 is Liu Xun; the literal English wrongly renders 鄩 as Zhen.
Tan stormed Weixian in Chuan, captured it, and presented the rebel generals Li Yan and Wang Kaiguan.
Tan stormed Weixian in Chanzhou, captured it, and presented the rebel generals Li Yan and Wang Kaiguan.
Chinese 澶州 is Chanzhou; idiomatic "Chuan" truncates the place-name and obscures the prefecture.
He was soon made deputy ambassador and acting commissioner of Tianping, with concurrent observation over Yan, Qi, and Cao.
He was soon made deputy ambassador and acting commissioner of Tianping, with concurrent observation over Yun, Qi, and Cao.
Chinese 鄆 is Yunzhou (Yun), not Yan; the idiomatic English misreads the prefecture name.
Soon he was appointed deputy ambassador of the Tianping army and acting military commissioner, concurrently Yan, Qi, and Cao circuit observation commissioner.
Soon he was appointed deputy ambassador of the Tianping army and acting military commissioner, concurrently Yun, Qi, and Cao circuit observation commissioner.
Chinese 鄆 is Yun, not Yan; the literal English misreads the prefecture name.
Soon he was posthumously enfeoffed Grand Preceptor, given the posthumous name Loyal Resolute, and buried on the Gaomen plateau in Kaifeng county.
Soon he was posthumously granted Grand Preceptor, given the posthumous name Loyal Resolute, and buried on the Gaomen plateau in Kaifeng county.
Chinese 冊贈 is posthumous bestowal of office/honor, not feudal enfeoffment; "enfeoffed" misstates 贈.
